Football dashboard

The big five European leagues — plus Allsvenskan — under the hood: standings, xG team analytics, player profiles and second-order insights.

Big five 2026/27 · Allsvenskan 2026TheSportsDB + Understat + FotMobUpdated 2026-09-14 11:09 (Stockholm)

Names marked like this open something — a club, a player, a match. The address bar follows you, so any card can be linked to.

What's new · 2026-09-13

2026-09-13

  • A missed call now says how near it was. Match reports and the report card show what chance the model gave the result that actually happened. That matters most for draws: a draw is almost never the single likeliest of three results, so the model almost never picks one — but a draw it gave 31% was a real possibility, and "missed" alone could not tell you that.
  • The model report card now grades against a fair yardstick. Hit rate and Brier score each sit beside what forecasting from home advantage alone would have scored on the very same matches, and the card says which dates it covers. It used to compare every league with one fixed number, which made a hard run of fixtures look like a bad model — Allsvenskan's card only began in August, the model's hardest weeks of the year.

2026-09-08

  • The team radar loses two spokes and gains a better one. It drew territory beside attack and box defence beside defence, which measure nearly the same thing — so every good side looked big everywhere and the shape said little. In their place: chance quality, how much a club makes of the territory it wins. Both old numbers are still in the table underneath.
  • A tale of the tape on every fixture. Pick an upcoming match and the two clubs are now compared on how they actually play at the venue this match is at — the home side from its home matches, the visitor from its away ones. Four rows rather than a fuller sweep, because most of the obvious extras just restate each other, and only the first two have a better end: on the style rows a longer bar means more of that thing, not better at it.

2026-09-05

  • Under the hood: the dashboard has tests. Twenty-three of them, covering the three ways this site has actually broken — a number the feed left out being read as a zero, a block showing the wrong season on an archive page, and sums that used to crash the nightly build. Nothing on the page changes; it should just be wrong less often.
  • The other ten players get a board. Every Allsvenskan outfielder with 450+ minutes, placed by the kind of defending he does — across, taking the ball off people; up, the clearing and blocking you only do in front of your own goal. Four leaderboards under it rank on one count each. There is no single "best defender" number, on purpose: adding the counts together just ranks centre-backs by how long their team spends pinned back.
  • The goalkeepers get a board. Every Allsvenskan keeper with 450+ minutes ranked by goals prevented — what the shots on target he faced were worth, against what he actually let in. Save percentage is in the table beside it because it is the one that misleads: it counts a tap-in and a shot from 25 metres the same, so it marks a keeper down for his defence.

2026-09-02

  • Allsvenskan gets a season shot profile. Two pitches per club in Team analytics — every shot it has taken this season, and every shot it has faced — with each dot where the shot was struck and sized by how good a chance it was. It shows the thing a single match report never can: who works the ball into the six-yard box, who shoots from 25 metres, and which defences only concede from distance.
  • Allsvenskan match reports now show when the chances came. A line per side climbing with every shot it took, so you can see who was on top and for how long — and whether the goals, marked on the lines, came with the run of play or against it.

9 older entries are in CHANGELOG.md in the repository.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

343 of 380 matches left to play. Points already won are kept as they are; every remaining fixture is simulated from current xG form.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

One panel per team, today's projected order · 35 nightly snapshots logged so far · each panel is scaled to its own range, so a small club's swings are as visible as a title contender's — read the badge, not the height, for the size of the move · green = projection has risen since its first snapshot, red = fallen · hover a dot for that night's title / European / relegation odds

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect and the backtest average is 0.583. Neither number means much on its own, because both move with how predictable the matches were. So each sits beside a yardstick scored on the same matches: every one of them forecast from nothing but this league's home, draw and away shares over the four years before the first graded call. Beating that column is the model earning its keep; it is also why the card no longer quotes one fixed base-rate figure for every league, since home advantage is not the same in any two of them. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

37 calls graded, 22 August 2026 to 13 September 2026 — 37 of the 37 matches this league has played in 2026-2027.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect and the backtest average is 0.583. Neither number means much on its own, because both move with how predictable the matches were. So each sits beside a yardstick scored on the same matches: every one of them forecast from nothing but this league's home, draw and away shares over the four years before the first graded call. Beating that column is the model earning its keep; it is also why the card no longer quotes one fixed base-rate figure for every league, since home advantage is not the same in any two of them. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Reading it. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect and the backtest average is 0.583. Neither number means much on its own, because both move with how predictable the matches were. So each sits beside a yardstick scored on the same matches: every one of them forecast from nothing but this league's home, draw and away shares over the four years before the first graded call. Beating that column is the model earning its keep; it is also why the card no longer quotes one fixed base-rate figure for every league, since home advantage is not the same in any two of them. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

279 of 306 matches left to play. Points already won are kept as they are; every remaining fixture is simulated from current xG form.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Predictions (xG Poisson model)

How to read this
Each club gets an attack and defence strength: a recency-weighted blend of 70% non-penalty xG and 30% actual goals, for and against (a match 180 days old counts half as much as one today — penalties are mostly noise, while real goals carry a club's persistent finishing skill). For a fixture, the home side's expected goals are its attack scaled by the opponent's defence relative to the league average, times a home-advantage factor measured from the league's own home/away xG split — and the same, mirrored, for the visitors. Feeding both expectations through independent Poisson distributions gives a probability for every scoreline, summed into the win/draw/win split shown in the bar. xG f'cast is each side's expected goals — deliberately not turned into a predicted scoreline, because chance quality says little about which exact score a match lands on and even the favourite scoreline rarely tops 15%. In the Understat leagues a small territory term also scales each attack by the club's deep-completions rate relative to the league average — validated on held-out seasons, unlike pressing intensity (PPDA), which was tried the same way, carried no extra signal, and stays out. Allsvenskan's feed has no deep-completions metric, so its model simply omits the term. Strengths reach back 1400 days — nearly four seasons — with that 180-day half-life doing the forgetting, a combination that beat a shorter hard-cutoff window on held-out seasons: an old match should fade, not fall off a cliff, because even faint evidence of how good a club is turns out to be worth keeping. Replaying every stored season with this exact recipe (backtest.py, 20,900 predictable matches) gives Brier 0.583 and 53% outcome accuracy, against 0.647 and 44% for guessing by league base rates.
A model, not a promise. These probabilities come from a small Poisson model over each club's recency-weighted chance quality (non-penalty xG, blended with a dash of actual goals) — nothing else. It has never heard of transfers, injuries, suspensions or new managers, and until the new season produces matches it leans heavily on last season's form. Clubs with no recent top-flight xG history at all have their fixtures left unpredicted. Backtested over 21,700 matches back to 2014/15 it calls the right result 53% of the time — clearly better than always guessing home win (44%), nowhere near clairvoyant. A conversation starter — never betting advice.

Season projection (2026-2027)

How to read this

What it does. Every fixture left in the season is played out 5,000 times using the same Poisson model as the predictions above, and the resulting final tables are counted up. Proj is the average final points total; the three percentages are how often a club finished first, in the top 4, and in the bottom 3.

Why it disagrees with the table. Points already banked are carried over untouched — they are real. Everything still to come is projected from recency-weighted non-penalty xG, which is mostly deaf to a hot finishing run. So a club sitting third on a thin xG record gets to keep its points and is still projected to fade, while a good side stuck in mid-table is projected to climb. The gap between the Now and # columns is that disagreement, in places.

Does it work? season_lab.py replays 58 finished seasons and projects the final table at ten points in each. Before a ball is kicked it lands 8.2 points per club from the final total; after a tenth of a season, 7.7 — against 18.8 for reading the table and multiplying, which at that stage is worse than simply assuming every club finishes on the league average. The model is ahead at every checkpoint right through to the final tenth, on held-out seasons its settings were never tuned on. Shrinking it back toward the table was tried and made it worse at every weight. Worth knowing: the preseason projection is already most of the way there. Updating it as results arrive is worth about 0.2 points per club after a tenth of the season, peaks near 0.7 at halfway, and is back under 0.2 by the run-in — most of what this table knows, it knew in August.

Reading the percentages. They are simulation frequencies, not certainties, and the top-four and bottom-three cuts are the site's own convention — real European and relegation places vary by league and by season. Anything under 0.5% shows as a dash.

Form, not news. The simulation knows only what clubs have done on the pitch. It has never heard of a transfer window, a sacking or an injury — when those things matter, they reach the projection the slow way, through results. It also assumes each club's current level holds for the rest of the season, which is exactly the assumption a January collapse breaks. A club returning after a year in the division below is projected on the last top-flight football it played, which may be a squad ago. A club scoring far more than its chances suggest is only partly credited for it — usually the right call, since across 1,170 historical team-seasons that kind of overperformance mostly evaporates, but the extreme cases (Sirius-scale runs included) regressed to roughly half their gap rather than to zero, and the model's discount was never tuned specifically for that tail.

270 of 306 matches left to play. Points already won are kept as they are; every remaining fixture is simulated from current xG form.

How wide is that projection?

How to read this

What it shows. The same 5,000 simulated seasons behind the Proj column above, but kept as a distribution of finishing positions instead of averaged down to one number. A short bar means the simulations agree; a long one means the run-in is still wide open for that club.

Reading it. The thick bar covers the middle half of simulated outcomes, the thin line the middle 90% — so a club whose thick bar sits entirely inside the shaded relegation band is in real trouble, while one whose bar straddles the line is still fighting it. The tick is the median finish, which is usually close to but not identical to the rounded Proj points figure above (points and rank are different simulation outputs).

Simulate one season

How to read this

What it does. Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect and the backtest average is 0.583. Neither number means much on its own, because both move with how predictable the matches were. So each sits beside a yardstick scored on the same matches: every one of them forecast from nothing but this league's home, draw and away shares over the four years before the first graded call. Beating that column is the model earning its keep; it is also why the card no longer quotes one fixed base-rate figure for every league, since home advantage is not the same in any two of them. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

Click the button and every fixture still to be played gets one simulated scoreline — each team's goals drawn from a Poisson distribution around the same expected-goals number (lam_home/lam_away) used everywhere else on this page — then the final table is built from real goals this time, not just win/draw/loss margins, so goal difference and the goals column are genuine tiebreakers rather than a coin flip. Click again for a different one.

Why it won't match the projection above. The Proj table is the average of thousands of these; any single run can and will put a mid-table side in the title race or drop a contender to mid-table, the same way any one real season can. That's the point of running it once instead of a thousand times — it shows what a plausible individual outcome actually looks like, not just the odds of it.

Plays every remaining fixture once, using the same expected-goals numbers as the projection above.

Projection over time

How to read this

What it shows. The season projection above is recomputed from scratch on every build, so on its own the page can only ever show tonight's opinion. This is every previous night's opinion too — one point added per team per night the projection ran, going back to the first snapshot logged this season.

Reading it. The number is projected final points, not the live table — it moves for two different reasons that look identical on the curve: a result banking real points, or the model simply revising its opinion of a club's remaining fixtures without a ball being kicked. Hover any dot for that night's title, European and relegation odds, which move for the same two reasons.

Why not just show probabilities. Title, European and relegation odds are usually a flat 0% or 100% for most of a season for most clubs — a true story for a handful of teams and a flat line for everyone else. Projected points moves for every club, contending or not, which is why it is the line and the odds are the hover.

One panel per team, today's projected order · 80 nightly snapshots logged so far · each panel is scaled to its own range, so a small club's swings are as visible as a title contender's — read the badge, not the height, for the size of the move · green = projection has risen since its first snapshot, red = fallen · hover a dot for that night's title / European / relegation odds

Model report card

How to read this
Every prediction the site publishes is written to a committed log the moment it is made, and frozen the instant a result exists — so this table grades calls that were on record before kickoff. That is a stricter test than the backtest, where the model's own settings were chosen by looking at the matches it is scored on. The Brier score is the squared error of the whole probability split, not just the top pick: 0 is perfect and the backtest average is 0.583. Neither number means much on its own, because both move with how predictable the matches were. So each sits beside a yardstick scored on the same matches: every one of them forecast from nothing but this league's home, draw and away shares over the four years before the first graded call. Beating that column is the model earning its keep; it is also why the card no longer quotes one fixed base-rate figure for every league, since home advantage is not the same in any two of them. The card grades only what was logged, and the log began partway through Allsvenskan's season, which matters more than it sounds: replaying the model over every Allsvenskan match since 2023, August and September were its hardest weeks — a Brier score of 0.631 pooled across those four seasons, against 0.597 to 0.604 in every other part of the year. A card that has only seen those weeks will read worse than the model is. Over whole seasons the same replay beats the home-advantage yardstick every time — 0.623 against 0.640 in 2024 and 0.605 against 0.654 in 2025 — so if this card shows the model behind it, that is a statement about the weeks it has seen rather than about the model. Calibration is the more revealing half of the table — a model can pick winners at a mediocre rate and still be well calibrated, which is what makes its probabilities usable. Once some calls have been revised between publication and kickoff, a further row re-scores the same fixtures using the first call the site ever published for them; if that number is close to the main one, the extra fortnight of data adds less than you would think. The skill or luck table scores the very same calls a second time, against Understat's post-match simulation of each fixture instead of against its scoreline: the Brier a call would have earned on average had the match been replayed from the chances both sides created. It is the one number here that can tell a bad model from a bad night, and it is pooled across the five leagues Understat covers because per league there are nowhere near enough graded calls to read. It is not a rival forecast — Understat's number exists only after the final whistle and knows every shot that was taken, which is exactly what makes it a fair standard to be judged against and a useless one to predict with.
A live scorecard, not the backtest. Every row here was published before kickoff and never edited, so unlike the backtest it cannot flatter the model with hindsight. Expect it to wander well above and below the backtested 53% for most of a season — a few hundred matches is still a small sample.

46 calls graded, 8 August 2026 to 13 September 2026 — 46 of the 165 matches this league has played in 2026.

Part of a season, not a season. The log began on 8 August 2026, so the 119 matches before it were never graded. A run of weeks can land on the hardest stretch of a season and read worse than the model is — or the easiest, and read better. The home-advantage column is scored on these same matches, which is why it is the fairer thing to compare against than any number from another stretch.

Matches

Pick an upcoming fixture to see both clubs side by side, or a match already played to see the score, what the chances were worth, and what the model said about it beforehand.

Match explorer

How to read this

What it shows. One match at a time, in either tense. An upcoming fixture gets everything the site knows about the two clubs gathered in one place: the model's win/draw/win call, both sides' recent form in results and in chance quality, their past meetings, the venue split that actually applies to this match, a tale of the tape, and each squad's leading attackers.

The tale of the tape is the one block here built only from the venue this match is at: the home side from its home matches, the visitor from its away ones, each ranked against the rest of the league at that same venue. That is not a detail — the median club creates about a fifth more chances at home than away and concedes about a fifth fewer, and only one season in ten runs the other way, so a profile averaged over every match quietly flatters whoever is travelling.

Four rows rather than a fuller sweep, because the obvious extra ones would repeat what is already there: chances created and territory won measure nearly the same thing, as do goals conceded and chances allowed near goal. Finishing is missing on purpose — it barely carries from one season to the next, so on a page previewing a match it is the number least worth knowing. The block needs five matches at that venue from both clubs, and eight clubs in the league to rank them against, so in the big five it appears around October rather than in August.

A match already played gets a report instead: the score, what the chances were worth on the day, and — the part worth coming for — what this site said about it beforehand, taken from the call written down before kickoff and never edited since. It is marked called it or missed on the day's actual result, and a miss also says what share the call gave the result that did happen. That second number is the fairer half of the verdict. It is the only half a draw can ever earn: a draw is almost never the single likeliest of three results, so it is almost never the call, and a draw given 31% was a real possibility the word “missed” would otherwise hide. A match that was never in a predictions slate says so rather than inventing a retrospective opinion; that is usually a promoted club with no top-flight xG history at the time. Form and squad lists are deliberately left off a report — they would describe the clubs now, not as they were then.

Match stats on a report are the team stat line both feeds keep for the 90 minutes, which is more than the xG the report used to show on its own. In the big five that is expected goals, non-penalty xG, deep completions (passes completed within about 20 metres of goal — territory rather than chances), PPDA (opposition passes allowed per defensive action: lower means more pressing, so its bar deliberately favours the smaller number) and expected points. Allsvenskan's feed measures far more, so its headline rows are expected goals, non-penalty xG, xG on target (which rates the shot rather than the chance, counting where in the goal it went), shots, shots on target, possession and expected points — with everything else the feed measured behind a disclosure under them: big chances and big chances missed, touches in the opposition box, xG split into open play and set play, corners, shots inside and outside the box, the woodwork, passes and pass accuracy, offsides, tackles, interceptions, blocks, clearances, keeper saves, duels and aerial duels won, successful dribbles, fouls and cards. The rows differ by league rather than being padded with blanks. The bar carries the comparison and the bolder number is the side ahead — except on the rows nobody wins, which are drawn faint and unbolded: tackles, blocks, clearances, saves, fouls and cards all climb with time spent defending, so a side can lead every one of them and be losing. Neither feed stores anything player-level per match, so there are no individual match ratings here; the player numbers on this site are season totals. A measurement neither side has is left off rather than printed empty — FotMob's xG on target is missing for whole matches at a time — and one only the away side has shows the home side a dash. A stat line that disagrees with the scoreline is dropped rather than shown: the two feeds would be describing different 90 minutes.

Where the shots came from is Allsvenskan only as well. FotMob records every attempt with the spot it was struck from and what a chance from there is worth, and each team gets its own picture of the last 36 metres of the pitch — which holds all but a handful of shots a season — both drawn attacking upwards. One circle is one shot and its area is its expected goals, so a circle twice as wide was four times the chance, down to a floor that keeps the faintest half-chances big enough to see: filled for a goal, filled paler for a save, grey where a defender blocked it, red where it hit the woodwork, and hollow for one that missed. The caption counts the shots, the ones on target and the expected goals they add up to. That last one can sit a little above the expected goals in the stat table, and the gap is not a mistake: FotMob discounts a shot taken straight after a save in the same passage of play, on the grounds that the chance has been counted once already, and adding the circles up one at a time does not. Hovering a circle names the player, the minute, the body part and what came of it; clicking one opens the same season card a name in the squad does. A shot from further out than the picture goes is drawn on its bottom edge rather than left out. Own goals are not on it at all — the feed records them at the other end of the pitch, under the man who scored one, with no expected goals — so they are counted in the caption of the team they were given to instead.

When the chances came is the same shots read along the clock rather than across the pitch, and it answers what the map cannot: a side that scored on eight minutes and defended for eighty, and a side that laid siege for eighty and got one back at the end, leave the same two numbers in the stat table. Each line climbs by one shot’s expected goals at the minute it was struck, both to the same scale, and a filled dot marks a goal. Stoppage time is played out rather than folded back into the 45th and 90th minute, so a shot on 45+3 is not drawn on top of one from the 48th. The dashed line sits after the last shot of the first half, which is as much of that half as the feed records: it keeps no stoppage figure of its own, so on a match where nobody had a shot in first-half stoppage — about half of them — the line falls on 45. The totals at the top are the same sums the map’s captions carry, and carry the same small gap to the stat table above.

Who played is Allsvenskan only, and it is the one thing that league gets which the big five do not: FotMob keeps a stat line per player per match, Understat keeps none at all. Both squads are listed as they were used — starters first, then whoever came off the bench — with FotMob’s rating out of 10, minutes, goals, assists, expected goals and assists, and shots, all for that match alone. Goalkeepers get their own line underneath for saves and goals prevented, which is xG on target faced minus goals conceded: a positive number is a keeper who saved more than the shots deserved. A name opens that player’s season card where the page holds one, because the match feed and the season squads share FotMob’s player ids and need no name matching. Anyone who did not get on is left out rather than listed with a dash.

The head-to-head on a report stops before the match being reported, so it shows the history the two sides actually brought into it.

The verdict is the same Poisson model as the Predictions block on the League tab, reading from the same numbers — the two can never disagree about a match. Its caveats apply here in full: no transfers, no injuries, no suspensions, no new managers.

Form is the last six matches, newest first, with the score and both sides' xG that day. It deliberately reaches back across the summer rather than showing an empty strip in August — a club's last six competitive matches are still the best short-term evidence there is, even if some were played in May. By venue shows each club at the venue it will actually be at — the home side's home record against the visitors' away record — with its record across all matches underneath, because a side that is excellent at home and ordinary overall is exactly the case the venue row alone would hide. Both cover a single season, named in the heading. In August that is still last season for a club that has not kicked off yet, and the two sides of a fixture can even be anchored to different seasons; the heading says which rather than calling it all 'this season'. The same goes for leading attackers, labelled per club, which falls back to the last completed season until this one has enough minutes in it to mean anything.

Head-to-head reaches back as far as the xG data goes — up to twelve seasons — and gives each meeting's score alongside what the chances were worth. A club that keeps losing these while winning the xG is a different story from one that is simply outplayed. It is kept deliberately neutral: no win/loss colouring, because this is the two clubs' shared history rather than a run of form belonging to whichever side happens to be at home this time — the winner of each meeting is marked on its name, and the tally names both clubs. Meetings in other competitions are not here; this is league data only.

What's missing is marked. A promoted club has no top-flight xG history, so the model declines to predict its fixtures rather than inventing a number, and its form and head-to-head sections say so instead of showing an empty table.

Preseason (club friendlies, FotMob)

Summer friendlies for the league's clubs — recent scores and the upcoming schedule. This tab only appears while friendlies are being played; once the season proper is under way it retires itself.

Friendlies lie. Preseason matches are played with rotated line-ups, experimental shapes and one eye on fitness — the results say little about the season ahead, and FotMob publishes no xG for them. This tab is for keeping an eye on what the clubs are up to over the summer, nothing more.

Team analytics (2026/27, Understat · Allsvenskan 2026, FotMob)

Metric glossary — what xG, npxG, xGBuildup, PPDA and friends actually mean
xG — expected goals
How good a team's or player's chances were. Every shot gets a value between 0 and 1: the probability that an average player scores from that spot and situation. A tap-in is ~0.9, a hopeful 30-metre hit ~0.02. Add them up and you get how many goals the chances “should” have produced.
xA — expected assists
The same idea for passing: the xG of the shot a pass created. A player who keeps serving up big chances gets a high xA even if teammates keep missing them.
npxG / npg — non-penalty xG and goals
xG and goals with penalties removed. A penalty is worth ~0.76 xG no matter who wins it, so stripping them out shows how much a player or team creates from open play.
G−xG — finishing
Goals scored minus expected goals. Above zero: converting chances an average finisher would miss. Below zero: missing chances that usually go in. Tends to swing back toward zero over time.
KP — key passes
Passes that led directly to a shot, whether or not it went in. Raw creativity volume, where xA measures the quality of what was created.
xGChain (xGCh)
Credit for being anywhere in a move that ended in a shot: the full xG of the chance is credited to every player who touched the ball in the build-up. Rewards involvement, not just the final pass or shot.
xGBuildup (xGB)
xGChain minus the shot and the assist pass. What's left is pure build-up play — deep-lying passers and defenders who start attacks score high here even with zero goals and assists.
PPDA — pressing intensity
Opponent passes allowed per defensive action in their half. Counter-intuitive direction: a LOW number means an aggressive press (the opponent barely gets 10 passes before being tackled), a high number means the team sits back.
Deep completions
Passes received within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal (crosses excluded). A good measure of sustained territory and box presence.
xPts — expected points
How many points a match “should” have given based on both teams' chances: the chance quality is converted into win/draw/loss probabilities and summed over the season. A team far above its xPts has been winning tight or lucky games.
npxGD — underlying dominance
Non-penalty xG created minus non-penalty xG conceded, per match. The single best summary of how well a team actually played, ignoring finishing luck at both ends.

xG table — results vs expected

How to read this

What it shows. Results next to what the chances say they should have been. xG (expected goals) values every shot by how often that kind of chance is scored; xPts converts each match's shots into win/draw/loss probabilities and sums the expected points.

How to read it. Pts−xPts above zero means the team banked more points than its chances deserved — running hot on finishing, goalkeeping or timing. npxGD is non-penalty xG difference (created minus conceded), widely considered the best single number for underlying strength: it predicts future results better than points do.

Caveat. xG is a model of chance quality, not truth — elite finishers beat it consistently, and one season is a small sample.

Team comparison

How to read this

What it shows. One to three teams overlaid on a radar of five style dimensions, each expressed as the team's percentile among the sides in that league. A single team is a profile rather than a comparison — that is where a click on a club's name over on the League tab lands, and it carries the club's last six matches underneath, because the radar says what kind of side this is and only the results say how it is going. Attack is non-penalty xG created per match and Defence is non-penalty xG conceded (flipped, so further out = fewer chances allowed). Finishing is goals minus xG — conversion above or below what the chances deserved. Pressing is PPDA flipped (opponent passes allowed per defensive action — fewer means a higher press). Chance quality is non-penalty xG per deep completion: what a side makes of the territory it wins, so a team that works the ball to the six-yard box sits far out and one that reaches the edge of the area and shoots from there does not.

Why five and not six. It used to draw Territory (deep completions per match) and Box defence (the same conceded) as two more spokes. Across 1,150 completed club-seasons Territory correlates with Attack at 0.87 and Box defence with Defence at 0.81 — near enough the same measurement twice — so any decent side bulged on both halves of both pairs and the shape was reporting how good a team is rather than what kind it is. Both numbers are still here, in the table underneath, where a restatement is a number rather than a shape. The worst-correlated pair left on the chart is Defence and Pressing at 0.50.

How to read it. The shape is the identity: a dominant pressing side bulges toward Attack–Pressing, a low-block counter team can look small here yet still win points on Finishing and Chance quality. The table underneath gives the raw per-match numbers behind each axis, the two that left it, and points against expected points. One caveat on Finishing: it is the one axis that does not carry — a club's goals-minus-xG repeats from one season to the next at about 0.22, where Attack repeats at 0.79 — so read it as what happened rather than as what this side is. Shots on target aren't in the data — Understat's team feed doesn't publish them — so chance quality (xG) stands in for shot accuracy.

Season by season. Under a single club, one row per season as far back as the data goes — where they finished, the record, goal difference, xG difference, and points against expected points. The bar is the gap between those last two: right and green means the club banked more than its chances deserved, left and red means it banked fewer. It is the luck quadrant from the Insights tab asked of a decade instead of a season, and it is what says whether a good year was a step up or a hot streak. A season spent in a lower division shows as a gap rather than being skipped, so the relegations are visible too. One caveat: the position is computed from the stored results, so it does not know about points deductions — Everton and Nottingham Forest in 2023/24, and Juventus in 2022/23, finished lower than this table puts them.

The squad. Under a single club, everyone who has played a minute for it in the season the page is about, most minutes first, with goals against xG and assists against xA. It lists players used, not a registered squad — neither feed carries a player until they have appeared — so a club one matchday into a season shows the eleven and its substitutes and grows to the mid-twenties by May. In the big five a name opens that player's profile card and career underneath; Allsvenskan's squads come from FotMob, which publishes no positions and nothing the player explorer is built on, so those names are listed rather than linked. It costs the page nothing in the big five — those players are already loaded for the Players tab, so the squad is a filter over them rather than a second copy.

Head-to-head mode. With exactly two teams picked, the card goes deeper: a tale-of-the-tape strip where each bar is split by the two sides' league-percentile share (the longer half leads, the number in brackets is the league rank as a percentile ordinal), this season's actual meetings between the clubs with the score and each side's xG that day, the last five results, points and non-penalty xG difference split by home/away, and both teams' rolling 6-match npxGD form curves overlaid on one chart — so you can see not just who is better on the season, but who is better right now, and what happened when they actually met.

Pick a team above for its style profile and recent form, or two or three to see them side by side. Picking exactly two unlocks a head-to-head deep dive: this season's meetings, a tale-of-the-tape bar duel, recent form, home/away splits and overlaid form curves.

Team style — pressing vs territory

How to read this

What it shows. Each team's playing identity in two numbers, averaged over the season. PPDA (passes per defensive action) counts how many passes a team lets the opponent play before making a tackle, interception or foul — fewer means a more aggressive press. Deep completions are passes completed within roughly 20 metres of the opponent's goal — a proxy for sustained territorial dominance.

How to read it. Top-left teams press high and pin opponents into their own box — the modern dominant style. Bottom-right teams sit deep and play direct, ceding the ball and the territory. Neither corner is 'better' — it's a style map, not a quality ranking. Hover a dot for exact values.

Form curves — rolling xG difference

How to read this

What it shows. Every team's underlying form across the whole season: non-penalty xG difference (chances created minus chances conceded, penalties excluded) averaged over a rolling 5-match window. Teams appear in final-table order and all curves share the same scale (±0.7), so shapes are directly comparable.

How to read it. Green stretches above the line are periods of outplaying opponents; red dips below are periods of being outplayed. Look for the story in the shape: a title challenge that faded after mid-season, a slow starter that clicked after a coaching change, a relegated team that was actually improving. The number after each name is the latest value; hover a curve for its season range.

Shot profile — where a season's chances come from

How to read this

What it shows. Every shot a club took over the season named above on the left, every shot it faced on the right, each drawn where it was struck. The match reports draw one match at a time; this is the same rows read the other way round, which is where habits show up rather than afternoons. A dot’s area is its expected goals — a dot twice as wide was four times the chance — down to a floor that keeps the faintest half-chance visible, and a filled dot is one that went in.

How to read it. Look at where the cloud sits before you look at how big it is. A side that works the ball into the six-yard box and one that shoots from 25 metres can take the same number of shots and be doing entirely different things: Sirius’s average attempt is worth 0.133 expected goals and Halmstads BK’s 0.085, which is a chance every 8 shots against one every 12. The right-hand pitch asks the same question of the defence — a back line that concedes only from distance is doing its job even when the shot count against it looks bad.

The set-play share in each caption is the share of the expected goals, not of the shots, that began at a stopped ball: a corner, a free kick, an attacking throw, or a set piece the feed does not break down further. A penalty is a stopped ball too and is deliberately not counted — one is worth about eight corners, so a single spot kick would move a club’s share further than a season of corners does, and the Insights tab has a block about penalties already.

Own goals are left out at both ends, as they are on the match map — the feed records them at the other end of the pitch, under the player who scored one, with no expected goals at all. This is Allsvenskan only: Understat publishes no shot locations for the big five, so there is nothing to draw for them.

Allsvenskan 2026, in league order. Both pitches are the last 36 metres, attacking upwards. one dot is one shot and its area is the chance it was, down to a floor that keeps the faintest visible; filled means it went in. All 16 clubs are drawn to one scale, so a bigger cloud really is more shooting.
